author: Ignatius of Antioch
addressee: Churches in Ephesus, Magnesia, Philadelphia, Tralles, Smyrna, the church in Rome, and Polycarp of Smyrna
occasion: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, writes while being taken under guard from Syria to Rome, where he expects to be martyred by wild beasts. He addresses churches that sent representatives to meet him and seeks to strengthen them against false teaching and division.
argument: Ignatius urges each church to unite around its bishop, presbyters, and deacons as the visible order willed by God. He warns against teachers who deny the real flesh, suffering, and resurrection of Jesus Christ, and against any return to Judaism. He presents his own coming martyrdom as the completion of his discipleship and asks the Roman church not to prevent it. Throughout, he grounds Christian unity and hope in the true incarnation, death, and resurrection of Jesus.

outline.move: Ignatius greets the Ephesian church and praises their bishop Onesimus and the companions who visited him.
He urges harmony with the bishop and presbyters, using the image of a choir and warning that those outside the altar lack the bread of God.
He warns against false teachers and praises the Ephesians for resisting them, describing Christ as the one physician.
He calls for prayer for others, humility in the last times, and recalls Paul's bond with Ephesus.
He urges frequent assembly for the Eucharist and teaches that faith and love are the beginning and end of life.
He warns that corrupters of households will perish, speaks of the Lord's ointment and the cross, and celebrates the hidden mysteries of Christ's birth, death, and the star.
He promises a second letter, describes the Eucharist as medicine of immortality, and asks prayers for the church in Syria.
Ignatius greets the Magnesians and praises their bishop Damas, urging respect for him despite his youth.
He warns against calling oneself a Christian without living it, and urges unity under the bishop, presbyters, and deacons.
He urges them to do nothing without the bishop and to abandon Judaism, since the prophets lived according to Christ.
He warns against Judaizing and old leaven, urges them to be established in the birth, passion, and resurrection of Christ, and speaks of his own bonds and their humility.
He urges submission to the bishop and presbyters, asks prayers for Syria, and sends greetings from Ephesus and Smyrna.
Ignatius greets the Philadelphians and praises their bishop, urging them to flee division and follow the shepherd.
He urges one Eucharist under the bishop and warns against listening to Judaizing teachers.
He recounts crying out in the Spirit to follow the bishop, and presents the gospel as the completion of the prophets.
He asks them to send a delegate to Antioch to rejoice with the church there, and greets them from Troas.
Ignatius greets Polycarp and exhorts him to care for his flock, bear with all, and be wise and watchful.
He urges Polycarp to stand firm against false teachers, care for widows and slaves, and instruct married couples.
He calls the church to follow the bishop, asks Polycarp to send a delegate to Syria, and sends greetings.
Ignatius greets the Roman church and begs them not to prevent his martyrdom, which he sees as his way to God.
He asks only for prayer, describes himself as God's wheat ground by beasts, and longs to be a true disciple.
He declares his desire to die for Christ, renounces love of the world, and asks the Romans to believe his words.
He asks prayers for the church in Syria and sends greetings from Smyrna.
Ignatius greets the Smyrnaeans and confesses the true flesh, suffering, and resurrection of Christ against those who say he only seemed to suffer.
He testifies that the risen Christ had real flesh, warns against false teachers as human-shaped beasts, and speaks of those who deny Christ.
He warns that even angels are judged without faith in Christ's blood, and urges all to follow the bishop in the Eucharist.
He urges honor for the bishop, thanks the Smyrnaeans for receiving his companions, and asks them to send a delegate to Antioch.
He sends greetings from Troas and greets individuals and households in Smyrna.
Ignatius greets the Trallians and praises their bishop Polybius, urging submission to the bishop, presbyters, and deacons.
He urges respect for the deacons and presbyters, and humbly refrains from writing about heavenly things.
He warns against heretical teaching and urges purity within the altar, that is, unity with the bishop.
He confesses the true birth, suffering, and resurrection of Christ, and warns against those who say he only seemed to suffer.
He asks prayers for himself and for the church in Syria, and urges love and submission to the bishop.

cast.name: Ignatius
cast.who: Bishop of Antioch, writing while a prisoner on his way to martyrdom in Rome.

cast.name: Onesimus
cast.who: Bishop of Ephesus, praised by Ignatius.

cast.name: Burrhus
cast.who: Deacon of Ephesus, later mentioned as accompanying Ignatius with the Ephesians and Smyrnaeans.

cast.name: Crocus
cast.who: A companion who comforted Ignatius and is called an example of the Ephesians' love.

cast.name: Euplus
cast.who: A companion who visited Ignatius with Onesimus, Burrhus, and Fronto.

cast.name: Fronto
cast.who: A companion who visited Ignatius with Onesimus, Burrhus, and Euplus.

cast.name: Polycarp
cast.who: Bishop of Smyrna, to whom Ignatius writes one letter.

cast.name: Philo
cast.who: Deacon from Cilicia who accompanied Ignatius.

cast.name: Rheus Agathopus
cast.who: A companion of Ignatius from Syria who renounced his former life.

cast.name: Alce
cast.who: A person dear to Ignatius, greeted in the letters to Polycarp and the Smyrnaeans.

cast.name: Attalus
cast.who: A person greeted by Ignatius in the letter to Polycarp.

cast.name: Tavia
cast.who: A woman whose household Ignatius greets in the letter to the Smyrnaeans.

cast.name: Daphnus
cast.who: A person greeted by Ignatius in the letter to the Smyrnaeans.

cast.name: Eutecnus
cast.who: A person greeted by Ignatius in the letter to the Smyrnaeans.

voices.speaker: The Spirit
voices.how_marked: Ignatius reports that the Spirit was proclaiming, with the content given in indirect discourse

voices.speaker: Jesus Christ
voices.how_marked: Quoted by Ignatius as speaking to those around Peter after the resurrection

voices.speaker: Opponents
voices.how_marked: Their views are paraphrased or quoted indirectly by Ignatius

scripture: The author uses the Septuagint (LXX) for Old Testament references and cites Psalms according to LXX numbering. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and Hebrew Psalm numbering where different (e.g., LXX Psalm 2 = Psalm 2; LXX Psalm 9 = Psalms 9–10; LXX Psalm 113 = Psalms 114–115; LXX Psalm 116 = Psalms 116–117; LXX Psalm 118 = Psalm 119; LXX Psalm 119 = Psalms 120–134; LXX Psalm 131 = Psalm 132; LXX Psalm 133 = Psalm 134; LXX Psalm 138 = Psalm 139; LXX Psalm 141 = Psalm 142; LXX Psalm 143 = Psalm 144; LXX Psalm 145 = Psalm 146; LXX Psalm 146 = Psalm 147; LXX Psalm 147 = Psalm 147; LXX Psalm 148 = Psalm 148; LXX Psalm 149 = Psalm 149; LXX Psalm 150 = Psalm 150).
uncertain: The exact date of the letters; the range c. 107–117 CE is widely accepted but not certain.
The precise route of Ignatius's journey from Syria to Rome.
The identity of some individuals mentioned only by name.
Whether the letters were written in the order they appear in the manuscript tradition.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Rheus Agathopus, source forms: Ῥέος Ἀγαθόπους
_unresolved_facts.fix: Ῥέῳ Ἀγαθόποδι (dative case; nominative would be Ῥέος Ἀγαθόπους, but the source shows dative Ῥέῳ Ἀγαθόποδι)
Εὔπλῳ (dative case; nominative would be Εὔπλους, but the source shows dative Εὔπλῳ)
Φρόντωνι (dative case; nominative would be Φρόντων, but the source shows dative Φρόντωνι)
Βούρρου (genitive), Βούρρῳ (dative) — the source never shows the nominative Βούρρος

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Κρόκος δέ, ὁ θεοῦ ἄξιος καὶ ὑμῶν, ὅν ἐξεμπλάριον
_unresolved_facts.fix: Κρόκος (nominative is correct, but note ὅν shows accusative usage in relative clause)
Δαμᾶ (vocative or undeclined form; nominative would be Δαμᾶς, but the source shows Δαμᾶ)
Ζωτίωνος (genitive; nominative would be Ζωτίων, but the source shows genitive Ζωτίωνος)
Φίλωνος (genitive; nominative would be Φίλων, but the source shows genitive Φίλωνος)
Πολύβιος (nominative is correct in 3.1, but note the source also has Πολύβιον in some manuscripts; the given form is acceptable)
Ἄτταλον (accusative; nominative would be Ἄτταλος, but the source shows accusative Ἄτταλον)
Δάφνον (accusative; nominative would be Δάφνος, but the source shows accusative Δάφνον)
Εὔτεκνον (accusative; nominative would be Εὔτεκνος, but the source shows accusative Εὔτεκνον)

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα ἐκήρυσσεν λέγον τάδε
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Spirit speaks in direct discourse in 5.7, but the brief should note this is reported speech by Ignatius, not independent direct discourse. The content 'Χωρὶς τοῦ ἐπισκόπου μηδὲν ποιεῖτε...' is presented as the Spirit's words.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἔφη αὐτοῖς: Λάβετε, ψηλαφήσατέ με καὶ ἴδετε, ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ δαιμόνιον ἀσώματον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The brief says 'Quoted by Ignatius as speaking to those around Peter after the resurrection' but the source says 'those around Peter' (τοὺς περὶ Πέτρον), not specifically 'Peter' alone. The brief is slightly imprecise.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου, ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source shows Ποντίου Πιλάτου (genitive) and Ποντίου Πιλάτον (accusative with error or variant), but the brief omits the praenomen Ποντίου 'Pontius' which is present in the source.
The source refers to John the Baptist (context of baptism), but the brief just says 'John' without specifying 'John the Baptist'.
The source says 'those around Peter' not 'Peter' directly; the brief simplifies to 'Peter'.
